deep.reconstruction:
Part A (terminology, continued from fol. 1v). Riemann criticises the German habit of translating both 'actio' and 'effectus' as 'Wirkung'. He notes that Kant tries to avoid the ambiguity by adding the Latin 'actio' or 'actio mutua' in brackets after 'Wirkung' or 'Wechselwirkung'. He considers possible German renderings: 'die Kraft ist gleich der Gegenkraft' for actio = reactio, and 'Satz vom kleinsten Kraftaufwande' for the principle of least action. Since German also lacks a simple word for 'agere', which he glosses as a striving directed at something else, he asks leave to use the foreign word. He adds that in his earlier writings Kant rendered 'actio' as 'Handlung'. This part contains no mathematics.

Part B ('Blatt 3': Molecularmechanik / Mechanica molecularum). Setting: free motion of point masses m_i with Cartesian coordinates (x_i, y_i, z_i), acted on by force components (X_i, Y_i, Z_i). The subscript 1 is used as a generic index.

(1) Newton's equations: m_i x_i'' = X_i, and likewise for y and z.

Reformulation: the accelerations a_i = (x_i'', y_i'', z_i'') are determined so that
G(a) = Σ_i m_i [ (x_i'' − X_i/m_i)^2 + (y_i'' − Y_i/m_i)^2 + (z_i'' − Z_i/m_i)^2 ]
is a minimum.

Proof given on the page:
(i) G ≥ 0, being a sum of squares with positive weights m_i. G attains its least value 0 exactly when every bracket vanishes, i.e. when (1) holds.
(ii) Conversely, suppose some bracket, say x_1'' − X_1/m_1, is nonzero. Vary x_1'' continuously so that its absolute value, and hence its square, decreases, while keeping all other accelerations fixed. Then G decreases, so the point was not a minimum. Hence the minimum is attained only when (1) holds.

Expansion (completed on fol. 3r). G differs from
H(a) = Σ m_i (x_i''^2 + y_i''^2 + z_i''^2) − 2 Σ (X_i x_i'' + Y_i y_i'' + Z_i z_i'')
only by a constant independent of the accelerations. [My filling-in:] that constant is Σ (X_i^2 + Y_i^2 + Z_i^2)/m_i. So minimising H is equivalent to minimising G.

Purpose. Fol. 3r ('Zurückführung der Bewegungsgesetze auf ein Ausgleichungsgesetz zwischen einander widerstreitenden Bestrebungen') shows the aim: recast the equations of motion as a minimum principle, a balancing of competing 'strivings'. The next step substitutes the potential forces X_i = ∂P/∂x_i, with P = Σ F(r_ii'), and multiplies by dt^2/4. This links the page to the preceding discussion of 'actio' and the principle of least action. The free-system case of Gauss's principle of least constraint is the starting point.
errors: No mathematical errors. The minimality argument is complete: a nonnegative weighted sum of squares, with a strict decrease whenever any single term is nonzero.

The difference between the two functions is stated without being written out. It is Σ (X_i^2 + Y_i^2 + Z_i^2)/m_i; it is independent of the accelerations, but not of the positions and time. 'Constant' here means constant with respect to the variables being minimised, which is correct in context.
The use of the subscript 1 as a generic summation index (Σ m_1 (...)) is notationally loose but clear. Fol. 3r switches to the index ι.

results.what: Newton's equations for a free point system are equivalent to minimising Σ m_i |a_i − F_i/m_i|^2 over the accelerations.
results.modern_name: Gauss's principle of least constraint (free, unconstrained case)
results.usually_credited_to: C. F. Gauss, 'Über ein neues allgemeines Grundgesetz der Mechanik' (1829)

results.what: Equivalent quadratic form Σ m a^2 − 2 Σ F·a, differing from the Gauss constraint by Σ F^2/m.
results.modern_name: Gibbs–Appell-type acceleration functional (S − F·a form) / completing the square

results.what: Philosophical-terminological remarks on actio/Wirkung, Kant's usage, and German renderings of action = reaction and least action.
results.modern_name: Terminology of the principle of least action / Newton's third law

deep.surprise_reason: The mathematics is the trivial free-system case of Gauss's 1829 principle of least constraint. Riemann was Gauss's student, so his knowing and using it is entirely expected. Fragments on Naturphilosophie and Molecularmechanik are known from the Nachlass and partly printed in the Gesammelte Werke. The only interest is the philosophical framing ('Ausgleichungsgesetz zwischen widerstreitenden Bestrebungen').

checkable.asserts: The Gauss constraint term differs from m a^2 − 2 X a by the acceleration-independent constant X^2/m.
The stationary point of the reduced functional is Newton's equation a = X/m.
The second derivative is 2m > 0, so the stationary point is a minimum.

checkable.sympy: a1,a2,X1,X2,m1,m2=symbols('a1 a2 X1 X2 m1 m2',positive=True); G=m1*(a1-X1/m1)**2+m2*(a2-X2/m2)**2; G.subs({a1:X1/m1,a2:X2/m2}) == 0
checkable.asserts: The constraint function attains its minimum value 0 exactly at the Newtonian accelerations (two-particle check).

The right margin carries a circled '(2)' and a pencil note, apparently '(Lit. Heft 2)' or similar, with a stroke pointing to the end of the Kant/Handlung paragraph. These are archival or editorial annotations missing from the transcription.

The page number '3.' at the top right is omitted.
In the minimality argument the image has 'd^2x_1/dt^2 - X_1/m_1'. The generic form 'd^2x/dt^2 - X/m etc.' is written without subscripts, as transcribed.
